title: Primary Function
learningObjectives: Connect the extension to crane load transfer.
student: State the structural function of the adjustable boom and telescoping extension.
instructor: The boom and extension position the hook and transfer the suspended load toward the mast-support system. The extension permits reach adjustment.

title: External Loads
student: Identify the load relevant to the local extension model and where it acts.
instructor: The assigned load is the downward hook load W, represented as concentrated at the free end of the effective local projection.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Distinguish the real support system from the local fixed section.
student: Identify the real support path through the boom, pivot, and hydraulic ram. Explain the local fixed-section idealization.
instructor: The real boom is supported by the mast pivot and hydraulic ram. Only the projecting extension beyond its support/retention section is isolated; that retention section supplies the local force and moment reactions.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the suspended load to the floor.
student: Trace the suspended load through the hook, extension, main boom, mast/support system, base, and floor. Identify where shear and bending occur.
instructor: The load passes from hook to extension, main boom, pivot/ram and mast, base, and floor. The local projection carries shear throughout and bending moment increasing toward its retained end.

title: Critical Location
student: Identify the critical section for bending in the local cantilever idealization and explain why.
instructor: The support/retention section is critical because the end load has its maximum lever arm there, producing maximum moment magnitude WL.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Keep the problem focused on flexural stress.
student: Identify the primary mechanical response. Why are mast buckling and connection stresses excluded?
instructor: The assigned response is longitudinal normal stress from local bending. Mast buckling and pin/bolt mechanics require different idealizations and are reserved for separate problems.

title: Relevant Parameters
student: Identify W, L, b, h, and t and explain how each affects the calculation.
instructor: W and L determine moment; b, h, and t determine area, second moment, and section modulus. All dimensions are assigned model values.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Create the local beam model before viewing the reference.
student: Draw only the effective projecting extension as a cantilever of length L with downward free-end load W. Show fixed-section reactions and the critical section.
instructor: A complete diagram shows the local projection, fixed retention section, downward end load, vertical reaction, reaction moment, and rectangular hollow section. It must not label the complete boom as a cantilever.

title: Modeling Assumptions
student: State the assumptions used to reduce the real crane to the local beam model.
instructor: Use static loading, a concentrated end load, a straight prismatic rectangular hollow projection, small-deformation linear-elastic beam stress, and assigned local geometry. Neglect self-weight, holes, welds, pins, mast and frame behavior, ram force, 3D effects, impact, swing, fatigue, vibration, and dynamics.

title: Analysis Plan
student: State the calculation sequence from equilibrium through internal resultants, section properties, bending stress, sensitivities, and interpretation.
instructor: Find reactions, Vmax, and Mmax; draw the moment diagram; calculate A, I, c, and S; calculate stress; evaluate load/reach/section sensitivity; and state limitations.

title: Boundary Conditions and Reactions
student: Determine the fixed-end reaction force and reaction moment generated by W.
instructor: R = W = {{crane_R_kN}} kN, and the reaction-moment magnitude is WL = {{crane_Mmax_kNm}} kN·m.

title: Internal Shear and Bending Moment
student: Determine Vmax and Mmax, including locations.
instructor: Vmax = {{crane_Vmax_kN}} kN and Mmax = {{crane_Mmax_kNm}} kN·m = {{crane_Mmax_Nmm}} N·mm. Both maxima occur at the local fixed section.

title: Bending-Moment Diagram
student: Sketch and label the bending-moment diagram for the local projection.
instructor: The diagram is triangular: zero at the free end and maximum magnitude {{crane_Mmax_kNm}} kN·m at the fixed section.

title: Cross-Section Properties
student: Calculate A, I about the horizontal centroidal axis, c = h/2, and S = I/c.
instructor: A = {{crane_A_mm2}} mm2, I = {{crane_I_mm4}} mm4, c = {{crane_c_mm}} mm, and S = {{crane_S_mm3}} mm3.

title: Maximum Bending Stress
student: Calculate maximum bending-stress magnitude using σmax = Mmaxc/I = Mmax/S.
instructor: σmax = {{crane_sigma_MPa}} MPa at the outer fibers of the fixed/support section.

title: Critical Fibers
student: Identify the maximum tensile and compressive stress locations and explain what reverses if moment direction reverses.
instructor: Maximum magnitudes occur at the outer top and bottom fibers, y = ±h/2. One face is tensile and the other compressive; reversing moment reverses their signs.

title: Load Sensitivity
student: Holding geometry fixed, determine how stress changes if W increases by 25%.
instructor: Because σmax is proportional to W, the stress increases 25% to {{crane_sigma_load25_MPa}} MPa.

title: Reach Sensitivity
student: Holding load and geometry fixed, determine how stress changes if L increases by 25%.
instructor: Because σmax is proportional to L, the stress increases 25% to {{crane_sigma_reach25_MPa}} MPa.

title: Section Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Explain height sensitivity of bending resistance.
student: Explain why increasing section height is generally more effective than a comparable small width increase for reducing bending stress.
instructor: Height appears cubed in the rectangular-section inertia terms and moves material farther from the neutral axis, strongly increasing I and section modulus.

title: Capacity-Mark Interpretation
student: Use M=WL to explain why longer reach generally requires lower allowable load. Why does this not establish a manufacturer rating?
instructor: For controlled allowable bending demand, increasing L requires decreasing W. Actual ratings also depend on frame and mast behavior, hydraulic capacity, connections, local stresses, stability, material strength, dynamics, and manufacturer requirements.

title: Model Limitations
student: List at least four excluded effects and explain why this stress is not a complete crane assessment.
instructor: Examples include frame reactions, ram force, pins, holes, welds, self-weight, mast behavior, tipping, material allowables, and dynamic lifting. Their exclusion limits the result to nominal local flexural stress.

title: Engineering Assessment
student: Report the governing location and stress, explain the reach-capacity relation, and identify one section modification that reduces stress without claiming a full redesign.
instructor: {{crane_assessment}}
